We prepared mesoporous TiO2 (anatase) films by spin-coating a solution of colloidal anatase particles onto a 30-nm-thick compact TiO2 underlayer. The underlayer was deposited by aerosol spray pyrolysis on a transparent-conducting-oxide-coated glass substrate acting as the electric front contact of the solar cell. Lead iodide (PbI 2) was then introduced into the TiO2 nanopores by spin-coating a 462 mg ml 2 1 ( , 1 M) solution of PbI2 in N , N -dimethylformamide (DMF) kept at 70 u C. The use of such a high PbI 2 concentration is critical to obtaining the high loading of the mesoporous TiO2 films required to fabricate solar cells of the highest performance.

A 20-40-nm-thick TiO2 compact layer was then deposited on the substrates by aerosol spray pyrolysis at 450 u C using a commercial titanium diisopropoxide bis(acetylacetonate) solution (75% in 2-propanol, Sigma-Aldrich) diluted in ethanol (1:39, volume ratio) as precursor and oxygen as carrier gas. After cooling to room temperature ( , 25 u C), the substrates were treated in an 0.04 M aqueous solution of TiCl4 for 30 min at 70 u C, rinsed with deionized water and dried at 500 u C for 20 min.

Figure 3b shows the incident-photon-to-current conversion efficiency (IPCE), or external quantum efficiency, spectrum for the perovskite cell. Generation of photocurrent starts at 800 nm, in agreement with the bandgap of the CH3NH3PbI3, and reaches peak values of over 90% in the short-wavelength region of the visible spectrum. Integrating the overlap of the IPCE spectrum with the AM1.5G solar photon flux yields a current density of 18.4 mA cm 2 2 , which is in excellent agreement with the measured photocurrent density, extrapolated to 17.9 mA cm 2 2 at the standard solar AM1.5G intensity of 100mWcm 2 2 .

This confirms that any mismatch between the simulated sunlight and the AM1.5G standard is negligibly small. Comparison with the absorptance or light-harvesting efficiency (LHE) depicted in Fig. 3c reveals that the low IPCE values in the range of 600-800nm result from the smaller absorption of the perovskite in this spectral region. This is also reflected in the spectrum of the internal quantum efficiency, or absorbed-photon-to-current conversion efficiency (APCE), which can be derived from the IPCE and LHE and is shown in Fig. 3d.

The APCE is greater than 90% over the whole visible region, without correction for reflective losses, indicating that the device achieves near-unity quantum yield for the generation and collection of charge carriers.

unresolved_notes: The evidence does not explicitly report the device polarity as n-i-p or p-i-n; polarity is therefore not_reported.

The source does not establish that the perovskite cell used for IPCE/LHE/APCE characterization was the same physical device as the typical Fig. 3a/Table 1 device, so it is retained as a separate individual device.

The certified device is explicitly one of several top-performance devices, but the source does not establish that it was the same physical device as the 15.0% best-performing cell; the two are kept separate. Being described as a top-performance device does not by itself establish champion status for the certified specimen.
The ten Table S1 cells are individually reported devices. Their reported average is represented separately as a population statistic rather than mixing the individual rows into the aggregate record.

The standard and slightly modified absorber-deposition settings produce the same reported finished architecture and absorber identity, so they remain one device family. The modified 5 s PbI2 spin-casting and 2-propanol pre-wetting values are retained on the explicitly identified best-performing specimen.

The source also applies the modified processing arm to a group of top-performance devices, including a reported PCE range, but the schema has no faithful field for group-only fabrication settings. Those group-level settings are therefore not assigned to every top-performance or certified specimen.

The family processing steps explicitly labeled as the standard procedure describe the reported baseline fabrication arm and should not be read as applying its 90 s PbI2 spin time or 20 s CH3NH3I dipping time to the modified top-performance arm.

The single-step comparison films, flat PbI2 films, mesoporous TiO2/PbI2 characterization specimens, and sequentially deposited comparison films on FTO are excluded because the evidence does not establish them as complete photovoltaic devices.
The complete photovoltaic device shown only by cross-sectional SEM supplies structural evidence for the device family and is not treated as another individually measured device.
No scan direction is supplied for the reported J–V or certified measurements.

The source rendering of the HTM formulation volumes ('28.8 m l', '17.5 m l', and '29 m l') and encapsulation thickness ('50m m-thick') does not unambiguously preserve the intended unit symbol; these raw values are retained without converting them to ml, mm, or µm.

The source reports both a 30-nm-thick compact TiO2 underlayer in the main preparation description and a 20-40-nm-thick compact layer in Methods. Both compatible source-reported quantities are retained rather than replacing either one.

The compact-layer thickness, mesoporous-layer thickness, TiO2 particle size, HTM overlayer thickness, and Co(III) dopant level are already represented as atomic family-level layer or constituent quantities, so family-1 was not replaced.
The metal-aperture-defined active area is a device property rather than a device-family property. It was retained or added only on supported individual devices.

The ten Table S1 rows report individual photovoltaic outcomes and therefore remain PerformanceObservation records rather than being moved into IndividualDevice.reported_properties or removed as unclaimed records.
